title: Fermented White Ant Sauce
author: Laker Grace
desc: White ants dewinged and left covered two days to ferment, then ground, rolled into small balls and dropped into salted boiling water to harden before groundnut paste goes in.
longDesc: This is the Acholi way with white ants and it is a different dish entirely from roasting them. The ants are dewinged, covered in a saucepan or bucket and left two days to ferment. Then they are ground, rolled into small balls, and dropped into water boiling with local salt, where they harden. Groundnut paste goes in and it is served with kalo. The fermentation is the step nobody expects, and the hardening of the balls is the doneness cue.
ingredients: Odi — peanut butter or groundnut paste
equipment: Saucepan or bucket with a cover
Grinding stone, or mortar and pestle
steps: Remove the wings from the ants.
Cover the ants in a saucepan or bucket and leave them about two days to ferment.
Roll the ground mixture into small balls.
Boil water and add the local salt, kadatona.
Add the balls and allow them to harden.
Add the peanut butter paste, odi.
chefTips: Two days covered is the ferment, and it is what separates this from every roasted-ant dish in the collection.
The balls harden in the salted boiling water, and that hardening is the cue. Until they firm up they will fall apart.
Kadatona is the local salt and it goes into the water before the balls, not after.
The odi goes in last. Groundnut paste boiled hard will split.
Roll the balls small. Large ones do not harden through.

This is one of several completely different Ugandan treatments of the same insect and they should not be confused: this Acholi fermented sauce; the Ganda roasted snack and pounded-to-flour luwombo base in UGA062; the Lango ground paste alakena in UGA094; and the Lugbara ombangulu in UGA099, pounded with salt and cooked in leaves.

A fried version exists alongside this one in the same source: roast the ants briefly to remove the wings, spread them in the sun to dry about ten minutes, sort out the remaining wings, fry them in a pan, add some salty water and let it boil off, and take them off when the water has dried up. That is a snack, not a sauce.
No quantities are documented. Nothing here is estimated.
commonMistakes: Adding the balls to unsalted water.
Lifting them out before they harden.
Boiling hard after the odi goes in.
sources: Adapted from 'Delicacy from the anthills', Daily Monitor, 4 August 2012, updated 9 January 2021 — which prints two non-overlapping methods and gives no quantities for either. The Acholi sauce method carried here is: remove the wings from the ants; cover them in a saucepan or bucket for about two days for them to ferment; when fermented, grind them and make small balls; boil water, add local salt called kadatona, then add the balls and allow them to harden; add peanut butter paste, odi, and serve with kalo.

The fried method in the same article, credited to Yoga Michael, chef at Sardina Restaurant, is given in the tips: roast the white ants briefly to remove the wings, spread them under the sun to dry for around ten minutes, sort them to remove the wings, put them in a pan and fry, add some salty water and leave it to boil off, and take it off when the water dries up. The two are not variants of one dish and are recorded separately.

A further Monitor article, 'Ugandans' insect menu beyond the nsenene delicacy', 4 January 2014, records three routes for enswa — roasted with a little salted water added on medium heat while stirring with a wooden ladle; boiled with salty water added before the pan goes on the fire; and dried then pounded into flour and prepared as luwombo. It gives no quantities anywhere.
The Ganda, Lango and Lugbara treatments of the same insect appear in this collection as UGA062, UGA094 and UGA099 and are drawn from separate sources.
reheating: Warm gently with a little water.
healthBenefits: Termites are high in protein, fat, iron and zinc.
Fermentation raises the availability of the minerals.
Groundnut paste adds plant protein and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Four Ugandan communities, one insect, four dishes that share nothing but the ingredient — fermented into balls in Acholi, pounded to flour for luwombo in Buganda, ground to a paste in Lango, pounded with salt and cooked in leaves in West Nile. If you want one example of why a Ugandan collection has to be organised by community rather than by country, this is it.
